note.text: Privatisation moves enterprise ownership from public to private interests, wholly or partly in the stated arrangement. It is distinct from liberalisation, which opens or changes competition rules, and commercialisation, which changes how an enterprise operates without necessarily selling it. Possible aims include finance, incentives or efficiency; concerns include access, market power, sale value and employment adjustment. Ownership change alone guarantees none of these outcomes. The lessons compare hypothetical policies rather than recommend a real transaction.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to distinguish privatisation from liberalisation or commercialisation and evaluate competing consequences. Builds on: nationalisation and mixed ownership. Leads to: judging scale and growth without assuming ownership alone settles performance.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: An invented authority sells part of an enterprise’s shares, retaining a public stake. Another authority keeps ownership but asks its enterprise to cover more costs through charges. These are different changes. A market can remain concentrated after an ownership sale, so describing it as private does not establish effective competition or low prices.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: State the direction and extent of ownership change. Ask about sale proceeds, continuing obligations, access and competition. Separate a short-term receipt from recurring profit or long-term service outcomes. Read whether a percentage refers to the whole enterprise or only a block of shares.

example: privatisation: a transfer from public to private ownership in the stated enterprise arrangement.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: Private investors buy part of a publicly held enterprise.
Rules allow additional suppliers without selling the existing public enterprise.
A publicly owned service changes charging and cost practices while ownership stays public.
The fictional sale leaves one dominant provider.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.
example: privatisation: That is the opposite ownership direction.
liberalisation: Competition rules and ownership are separate dimensions.
commercialisation: Operating methods can change while ownership remains unchanged.
market-power concern: Ownership and the number or strength of competitors are different issues.

questions.prompt: A fictional state-held block contains {total} identical shares. Under the stated sale, {sold} shares move to private ownership. What percentage of that original block remains publicly held?

misconceptions.explain: That is the sold private portion, not the public remainder.
That is the share count, not a percentage of the original block.

solution: As a percentage of the original block: {total-sold}/{total} × {100} = {answer}%.
